 The Education Department is allowed to move student-loan borrowers off an affordable repayment plan, a new legal filing said.
 A federal judge this week denied a motion filed by the law firm Public Goods Practice to stop the forced transfer of borrowers off the SAVE repayment plan.
 The Trump administration eliminated SAVE — a Biden-era plan that allowed for cheaper payments and a shorter timeline to debt relief — and started sending notices to enrolled borrowers in July with a 90-day timeframe to transition off the plan. If they did not move within their timeframe, the Education Department said, they would be automatically placed on a standard plan with the most expensive payments.
 Judge Loren Alikhan wrote in her ruling that the plaintiffs did not sufficiently establish harm, thus permitting the department to involuntarily move borrowers off SAVE. The case, however, is still ongoing — the ruling did not decide on the merits of the lawsuit, including whether borrowers should receive the relief they might have qualified for under SAVE before it was eliminated.
 While the department emphasized a 90-day timeframe to leave the plan, the deadlines have shifted. After 90 days, borrowers received a "final notice" extending their timeframe by an additional 30 days. The notice told borrowers this was their last opportunity to switch plans before being placed in a standard plan. However, some borrowers who remained on SAVE past their final 30 days told Business Insider they have remained in forbearance, and no action has been taken on their accounts.
 Public Goods Practice filed a request earlier this month to provide details on the timeline for the transfer. The law firm said in its filing that, when it asked the Education Department's counsel about timing for the transfer, it said it didn't "'know when borrowers whose 30-day period has expired will be moved to new plans.'"
 The department has not commented on its plans to involuntarily move borrowers off SAVE.
